item.title: DairySocialTwin: Auditing the video-to-graph evidence chain in cattle social networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.32989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Video-derived social graphs can appear precise while inheriting uncertainty from detection, tracking, classification, and aggregation. We present DairySocialTwin, a graph-centered audit framework applied to 203 videos (122 h 23 min) from 15 views at three commercial dairy farms. Curation retained 447 of 839 candidate clips; 400 entered a frozen source-clip index, including 71 legacy clips with unavailable farm and time metadata. Five models were compared on a development split, with an NRI-style model retained as an exploratory trade-off between class balance and dyadic output. In a 90-min manual audit, reconciliation improved switches, fragmentation, and continuous-track duration across three gap definitions, but constrained identity capacity and inherited detector errors limited claims of identity accuracy. Matched manual and reconciled summaries showed coarse agreement and assignment sensitivity. Camera-specific semantics, observation opportunity, and identity-summary-to-video trace-back made these dependencies inspectable. DairySocialTwin supports auditable relational inference without claiming permanent identity, calibrated behavior, or biological diagnosis.
item.dc:creator: Yiwen Huang, Suresh Raja Neethirajan

item.title: False Belief Dissemination, Persistence and Mitigation in Multi-Agent Social Networks Through the Lens of the Mandela Effect
item.description: arXiv:2610.33026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent social networks are emerging as communities in which agents communicate, retain memories, and publish information that others can find as evidence. These interactions create opportunities for false claims to spread and remain influential beyond their original sources, analogous to the Mandela effect in human societies, in which many people recall the same false memory. In this paper, we systematically study false-belief dynamics through the lens of the Mandela effect, focusing on dissemination, persistence, and mitigation. Specifically, we build a controlled framework connecting agent communication, private memory, and a shared simulated web to mimic information dissemination in practical social networks, supported by 540 fabricated claims spanning 8 domains and 4 plausibility levels. For dissemination, we measure how widely and quickly claims gain acceptance across models and communication topologies. For persistence, we withdraw agents promoting fabricated claims while retaining existing articles and memories, and track subsequent acceptance. For mitigation, we compare preventive measures applied before implantation with corrective interventions introduced after claims have spread. Experimental results show that evaluated models readily accept and disseminate fabricated claims, with dissemination reach as high as 96.0%. Dissemination reach varies with claim plausibility, domain, and network size and composition, while communication topology shapes dissemination speed across model families. Acceptance barely declines after fabricators withdraw, and targeted corrective interventions outperform the preventive measures without eliminating false beliefs. These findings identify persistent false beliefs as a safety challenge for multi-agent social networks and highlight the need to address both their initial dissemination and the accumulated evidence that sustains them.
item.dc:creator: Dianzhi Yu, Hongru Wang, Ziheng Xiong, Yanyu Chen, Zixing Song, Jianting Chen, Zhenfei Yin, Jeff Z. Pan, Amos Storkey, Irwin King

item.title: Algorithmic Fairness for Influence Maximization: A Survey of Models, Metrics, and Optimization Techniques
item.description: arXiv:2610.33034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Influence maximization (IM) has become a basis of modeling information spread across social networks, with applications in viral marketing, public health, and political campaigns. However, classical IM algorithms often prioritize the spread of overall influence and ignore its fairness, resulting in disadvantages for marginalized or underrepresented communities. This survey provides a detailed look at fairness-aware influence maximization, focusing on important challenges, models, and methods designed to ensure fair influence maximization. We categorize existing methods into five groups based on their fairness objectives, including parity, diversity, and utility, and discuss how they handle biased network structure, protected attributes, and seeding constraints. We also examine how fairness-aware influence maximization methods perform on real-world data to highlight the importance of combining fairness with classical influence maximization methods. By bridging the gap between influence spread and social equity, this survey lays the foundation for designing fair algorithms that ensure fair representation in large-scale diffusion processes. The survey concludes by outlining emerging trends, open challenges, and prospective future directions in the domain, highlighting the need for expertise spanning multiple disciplines.
item.dc:creator: Shashank Sheshar Singh, Sunil Kumar Meena, Kuldeep Singh, krati Saxena

item.title: An autocomplete model for elections
item.description: arXiv:2610.33035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider two linked problems for ranked choice elections: building a compact summary of a preference profile $P$, and generating synthetic profiles that resemble $P$ in key ways. We introduce a Markov model based on which candidate names follow which on observed ballots and record this in a succession matrix on candidates together with a start/stop symbol. This provides the basis for new ``autocomplete'' methods for generating synthetic profiles, with ballot length that can be tuned to a target. We compare succession-based generation to parallel use of summaries built from positional frequencies and head-to-head comparisons. To execute this comparison, we introduce new descriptive statistics of profiles that allow new tests of whether synthetic profiles are realistic. In experiments on Scottish ranked-choice profiles, succession-based generation captures held-out ballot structure well, performs especially strongly when completing partial ballots, and often preserves election outcomes, outperforming the alternatives on all counts. Finally, we study the dynamics of iterating the train-and-generate process.
item.dc:creator: Moon Duchin, Kristopher Tapp

item.title: A Multimodal Framework for Measuring Creator Communication on Short-Form Video
item.description: arXiv:2610.33043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Short-form video combines speech, imagery, and on-screen text, creating challenges for systematic content analysis. We present a five-stage multimodal framework for measuring creators' themes and communication strategies at scale. The framework integrates platform metadata, speech transcripts, and vision-language descriptions of sampled frames, then applies large language models to generate predefined indicators and open-ended labels. An audited keyword scheme consolidates thematic labels, while creator-weighted aggregation gives each account equal weight regardless of posting volume. We demonstrate the framework on 9,852 TikTok videos from sixteen creators, retaining 7,311 videos for analysis across seven themes and seven communication indicators. Automated profiles reveal substantial differences in creators' use of education, humor, and responses to current events. Validation against two independent expert annotators yielded a mean framework-expert agreement of Cohen's $\kappa = 0.40$ across the six binary indicators, close to the $\kappa = 0.42$ the two experts achieved with each other, though agreement varied substantially across individual indicators. The framework provides a modular approach to comparative analysis of creator communication, combining scalable annotation with transparent aggregation and construct-specific validation.
item.dc:creator: Julie R. Ancis, Michael Fire, Omer Tarshish

item.title: Learning the Past from the Future: Retrospective Reconstruction in Temporal Interaction Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.33171v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal link prediction uses past interactions to predict future links. In practice, interaction records from web and mobile applications can contain gaps caused by logging failures, API limits or lost records, even when later events remain available. To our knowledge, the extent to which later events help recover interactions within such gaps has not been measured directly for this ranking task. We study retrospective reconstruction using the tgbl-wiki and tgbl-comment datasets. We hide a two-hour window, use its interactions as ground truth, and rank the directed pairs active within it. We compare count-based heuristics and logistic regression models using past information alone or together with 1, 6 or 24 hours of later events. Target pairs and candidate lists remain fixed across conditions, so differences in ranking performance cannot be attributed to changes in candidate selection. With 24 hours of later events, the 26-feature logistic regression improves mean reciprocal rank (MRR) by 0.039 on tgbl-wiki under exhaustive ranking, 0.046 under historical-random ranking, and 0.108 on tgbl-comment under historical-random ranking. The 26-feature logistic regression benefits from adding later features to past features, whereas replacing the past pair count with the later pair count reduces MRR by 0.157 on tgbl-wiki under exhaustive ranking. A control removing later interactions from query sources to historically observed destinations reduces the MRR gain by 59% on tgbl-wiki and 10% on tgbl-comment. Because this control removes more than repeated target pairs, these reductions cannot be attributed to pair recurrence alone. Later events improve the ranking of hidden interactions on both datasets, including tgbl-comment, where only 6.4% of target pairs reappeared within 24 hours.
item.dc:creator: Amarnath R

item.title: Measuring Psychological Constructs from Social Media Text Using the Word Embedding Projection Approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.33677v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Social media text offers new opportunities for tracking psychological constructs over time, but such measurement requires methods that are interpretable and stable in longitudinal settings. Grounded in Conceptual Space Theory and semantic projection, this study develops the Word Embedding Projection Approach (WEPA), which represents psychological constructs as semantic axes defined by theory-driven anchor words in a domain-specific word embedding space. WEPA scores are interpreted as indicators of expressed psychological salience in user-generated text. Using panel data from Keep, a Chinese fitness-oriented social media platform (177,829 users; 2,668,298 weekly observations), we evaluate WEPA across four studies. Study I examines the measurement foundation through anchor-word validation, human-coded benchmarks, and cross-temporal semantic-axis stability checks. Studies II and III show theoretically interpretable predictive associations between WEPA-derived scores and subsequent exercise duration for goal-setting constructs and the four source dimensions of self-efficacy. Study IV provides exploratory relative-week trajectories of aggregate construct dynamics. Overall, WEPA shows strong agreement with human-coded benchmarks for goal specificity and physiological states and achieves broader text coverage than a dictionary-based baseline. These findings suggest that WEPA offers a promising approach to theory-driven psychological measurement from domain-specific social media text.
item.dc:creator: Xudong Deng, Yijun Li

item.title: Resource competition and survival for random walkers on complex networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.33831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problem of $W$ random walkers on a complex network where each walker requires an amount $\theta$ of resource at each time to survive. Resource is stochastically produced at each vertex of the network with a specified distribution. The survival time of the system of walkers is defined as the time required for all $W$ walkers to die. Using numerical simulations, we show that Erd{\H o}s-R\'enyi networks a have higher mean survival time than Scale-free networks as expected, but also that uniform distribution production leads to higher mean survival time than exponential distribution with the same mean. We derive an exact expression for the survival-time distribution under the assumption of independent walker lifespans, and use it to show that scale-free network topology produces strong dependence in the lifespans but homogeneous topology does not. We moreover demonstrate how the survival time can be substantially increased without changing the resource production or network topology by appropriately biasing the movement of the walkers towards low degree vertices on Scale-free networks, but has no effect on Erd{\H o}s-R{\'e}nyi networks.
item.dc:creator: Snehal Shekatkar

item.title: Fear Doesn't Go Viral, It Lingers: Spread, Affect, and Discourse of Food-Fear Content on TikTok
item.description: arXiv:2610.33898v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: TikTok has become a primary channel for nutrition information, and alongside evidence-based content, it hosts a growing stream of \emph{fear-based} wellness messaging that frames ordinary foods as ``toxic,'' ``poison,'' or things to ``never eat.'' Prior work has extensively studied political and public-health misinformation and audited the accuracy of health videos, but to the best of our knowledge, no work has examined how everyday food-fear content spreads and how audiences respond to it. To investigate this, we collected 97,234 TikTok food and nutrition videos, labeled them \textit{Fear} or \textit{Non-Fear} with a zero-shot multimodal classifier built on Gemini~3 Flash that is validated against human consensus (Cohen's $\kappa=0.81$), and analyzed more than 1.1M comments and 272K parent-reply pairs. Contrary to the intuition that fear ``goes viral,'' fear videos reach fewer people than non-fear videos. Their distinctive signature lies in dynamics: they are shared more per view (1.7--2.1$\times$ after controls) and their discussion persists longer (comment half-life 1.62$\times$ after controls). These shifts are modest in size but hold after controlling for reach. Comments on fear videos are more negative, angrier, and more disgusted, yet negativity is \emph{not} more self-reinforcing: negative comments draw negative replies at the same rate as in non-fear threads, while positive comments are far less likely to stay positive. Fear threads are contested rather than one-sided, with both more corrective and more alarm-amplifying replies. Fear discourse concentrates in frames about industrial ingredients, contaminants, and institutional distrust, and its repertoire of frames widens over 2020--2026. Our results argue for persistence-based rather than virality-based signals when platforms seek harmful health content.
item.dc:creator: Hunjun Shin, Hongpeng Fu, Divya Chaudhary, Mohit Singhal

item.title: The Hidden Costs of Gatekeeping in Open Science: Quasi-Experimental Evidence from arXiv's Endorsement Policy Tightening
item.description: arXiv:2610.33980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Preprint servers and open science platforms have become core infrastructure through which scientific knowledge circulates on the Web, greatly facilitating the dissemination and diffusion of online scientific information. Yet to safeguard content quality, many of these platforms rely on existing members to vouch for newcomers; how such network-mediated gatekeeping reshapes entry barriers across different scientific communities remains systematically underexplored. To address this, I examine the potential unequal impacts of this mechanism through arXiv's tightening of its endorsement policy in early 2026. Using the metadata of three million arXiv papers and the co-authorship networks of each research community, I compare the influx and dynamics of first-time submitters before and after the policy across eight disciplines. The findings show that the policy reduced the entry of new authors, and this reduction was concentrated in fields where co-authorship ties are sparse, while fields with dense collaboration networks were largely spared. A comparison with a parallel preprint server in biology suggests that this likely reflects a shift in where researchers choose to post rather than a decline in research activity. These findings demonstrate that the network structure of a scientific community shapes who can enter online scientific production, advancing our understanding of how the Web's open knowledge infrastructure shapes inequality in the diffusion of science.
item.dc:creator: Wenchang Wang

item.title: The golden cage of science: first-last author prestige gap buys impact over disruption
item.description: arXiv:2610.34020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: First and last authors make critical but distinct contributions in the majority of scientific papers. First authors tend to conduct research and analysis, whereas last authors are usually responsible for setting research directions and providing resources and supervision. The first-last author prestige gap (FL gap, $\Delta H$) is defined as the H-index difference between the last and first authors prior to the focal paper's publication. The FL gap serves as a measure of the prestige asymmetry between the two dominant collaborators. We find that larger FL gaps in either direction are associated with higher impact and lower disruption. This trade-off is robust across team sizes and intensities of prior collaboration and can not be explained by first and last authors' separate prestige effects or their academic age gap. Further analysis shows that variation in last author prestige is associated with larger differences in both the article's impact and disruption than variation in first author prestige. We refer to this coexistence of higher impact and lower disruption related to the FL gap as the ``golden cage of science'', which reflects a common collaboration structure that statistically produces highly cited but less disruptive work. These findings suggest the first-last author prestige gap as an important indicator for examining how research teams balance senior guidance with exploratory autonomy.
item.dc:creator: Chi Zhang, Yilin Bi, Tao Zhou

item.title: Investigating Forecasting Capabilities of Narrative Networks on Emerging Stories
item.description: arXiv:2610.35628v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Networks have been used to model the interactions among the elements that underlie a narrative. In this paper, we investigate whether the structure of these networks can predict which links will emerge as a storyline evolves. We construct these networks from news articles using a Semantic Edge Parser (SEP) built on a Large Language Model (LLM), and evaluate the networks on three disparate real-world storylines, the 2022 Canadian Freedom Convoy, Hurricane Melissa (2025), and the 2025-26 Iranian protests. To test the narrative network's predictive capability, we construct a rolling window of the narrative and predict the emergent links between existing narrative elements on the day following the rolling window period. We identify candidate links with seven standard link predictors, including the Adamic-Adar index, Common Neighbors, and Preferential Attachment. Forecasting next-day links across the three storylines, we find Preferential Attachment to be the strongest standard link predictor, achieving a mean ROC-AUC of 0.76-0.79. It exceeds EdgeBank, a memorization baseline, by 11.3-14.5 points on every event. To summarize, narrative-network structure ranks next-day emergent relations above chance, though this advantage is concentrated among the most frequently mentioned, highly connected entities.
item.dc:creator: Ravi Teja Karumuri, Steven Corman, Huan Liu, Joshua Garland

item.title: LLM-Augmented Agent-Based Simulation of Cyber Social Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.32988v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Social media bots are often portrayed as malicious automations to be detected and removed, but automation on social media platforms encompasses a wide spectrum of roles, behaviors, and rhetorical strategies that can shape online discourse in both constructive and destructive ways. This work conceptualizes these automated actors as \textbf{Cyber Social Agents} through a taxonomy of archetypes characterized by their operational tactics and rhetorical style. We integrate this taxonomy into an LLM-driven social simulation, where agents communicate and coordinate in a network environment. Using empirically grounded CSA personas, we simulate heterogeneous online societies to study how agent diversity shapes information diffusion and social influence. Our approach bridges the gap between rule-based agent models and LLM-powered simulations with generated agents that are parameterized from empirical data.
item.dc:creator: Lynnette Hui Xian Ng, Kathleen M. Carley

item.title: From Data Footprints to Researcher Fingerprints: Temporal Ego-centric Research Group Detection in Scientific Knowledge Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.34313v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding who researchers collaborate with, when and how their research groups form, and how these evolve over time is a foundational prerequisite for constructing multidimensional, evidence-based researcher fingerprints -- a requirement that has become increasingly urgent in the context of ongoing reforms in research evaluation advocated by initiatives such as DORA, the Leiden Manifesto, and CoARA. In this paper, we propose an egocentric approach for fine-grained research group detection, operating at the scale of individual researchers' ego networks, as extracted from Scientific Knowledge Graphs (SKGs), and requiring the ego node to be present in all identified research groups -- a constraint that is not merely technical but reflects a commitment to researcher-centred analysis. Our approach builds on the Leiden algorithm as its computational core and is grounded in SKGs, which provide the heterogeneous, open scholarly metadata necessary to trace collaboration patterns at scale in a reproducible and transparent manner. We evaluate the proposed method through a user evaluation involving 10 researchers with diverse backgrounds and career stages, demonstrating its ability to surface meaningful and interpretable collaboration structures. The research groups identified constitute the structural scaffold upon which richer characterisations of scholarly identity -- including roles, seniority, contribution types, and publication patterns -- can be built in subsequent work, contributing to the broader goal of fairer and more transparent research assessment.
item.dc:creator: Simone Angioni, Miriam Baglioni, Andrea Mannocci, Paolo Manghi

item.title: Joint Independence Testing for Latent Position Random Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.34544v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Kernel techniques are among the most powerful methods in data science and statistics. One of the key properties of kernels contributing to their numerous successful applications is that the associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space is expressive enough to encode probability distributions without loss of information or to capture the joint independence of $M\ge 2$ random variables, under mild conditions. Computationally, these measures (i) rely on the so-called Gram matrix which contains the pairwise similarity of sample points, and (ii) converge at a rate $O \left(n^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)$, where $n$ denotes the sample size. We focus on measuring the independence of latent position random graphs (LPRGs), a model widely-applied for instance in neuroscience, sociology, and epidemiology. In LPRGs a latent representation is associated to each node. The similarity of these representations (meant via a kernel) determines whether two nodes are connected, making the Gram matrices only implicitly observable and the estimation challenging. Despite the fundamental importance of quantifying the independence of $M$ LPRGs, very little is known about the solution of this problem; existing techniques are restricted to $M=2$ components and only guarantee consistency without rates. In this work, (i) we define an independence measure called graph Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion (GHSIC) for $M\ge 2$ LPRGs, (ii) we prove that it can be estimated at a rate $\tilde{O}\left(n^{-\frac{1}{3}}\right)$ relying on spectral decomposition of adjacency matrices, (iii) without the need to choose kernels and their hyperparameters. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed GHSIC estimator both on synthetic examples and in the analysis of brain functional connectivity subnetworks in natural language perception.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyi Wen, Zoltan Szabo

item.title: AskGLP1: A Knowledge Graph LLM Agent for Exploring GLP-1 Experience from Online Patient Narratives
item.description: arXiv:2610.34987v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: GLP-1 medications are increasingly used for weight management, and many people share their experiences online. These narratives show why people take the drugs and what they experience, but they remain unstructured and disconnected from formal pharmacovigilance. We therefore present AskGLP1, a system that transforms online patient narratives into a knowledge graph (KG) and answers questions about medication experiences. Through an LLM-assisted pipeline grounded in the MedDRA terminology, AskGLP1 screens nearly 8.5 million Reddit posts for medication experiences and distills 163,135 of them, with 2,506 WebMD reviews, into a KG of 385,790 drug-side-effect and drug-purpose relations. We find that GLP-1 experiences are source- and drug-specific. Online narratives share the most common gastrointestinal symptoms with FAERS, but they foreground everyday burdens such as fatigue and food aversion, whereas FAERS reports more often include injection-site reactions and selected serious diagnoses such as pancreatitis. We further find that posts report less nausea and vomiting for tirzepatide than for semaglutide, more fatigue for Wegovy than Ozempic and for Zepbound than Mounjaro. Evaluations show that the agent answers with verifiable evidence and declines requests for medical advice. Our findings reveal gaps between what FAERS captures and what people report online, and they call for patient-centered approaches to pharmacovigilance. Code, prompts, and evaluation questions are available at https://github.com/ZhaoqianXue/AskGLP1.
item.dc:creator: Zhaoqian Xue, Anay Somani, Siddhartha Singh, Junting Mu, Zhongyin Wang, Haozheng Liu, Ayesha Khatun, Yeaeun Kwon, Renkai Ma, Siyuan Ma, Zhe He, Danxia Yu, Lingyao Li

item.title: ArchiveLens: A Generative Spatial Knowledge Framework for Semantic Reconstruction of Historical Maps
item.description: arXiv:2610.35606v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Historical maps contain dense morphological and semantic information about past urban environments, but many digitization workflows focus primarily on extracting geometry, and do not capture cartographic semantics such as building use and construction materials. This study introduces ArchiveLens, a generative spatial knowledge framework that operationalizes historical maps as entity-centric, machine-queryable geospatial databases. The pipeline decouples morphological and semantic reconstruction through three stages: tiled YOLOv11-seg instance segmentation for building footprint extraction; deterministic material classification via hue, saturation, and value (HSV)-based color thresholds; and localized attribute parsing using a quantized vision-language model constrained by domain-specific prompts. Extracted entities are integrated into a hybrid Spatial-Temporal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (ST-RAG) architecture that combines dense semantic retrieval with symbolic spatio-temporal filtering and mandatory provenance grounding. Applied to 445 georeferenced Sanborn map sheets of Chicago (1918-1950), the framework achieves high geometric and semantic accuracy. Beyond performance, ArchiveLens advances GIScience by formalizing historical cartography as structured spatial knowledge representation, allowing researchers to query building attributes and compare spatial patterns across map sheets and years.
item.dc:creator: Yanan Wu, Yalin Yang, Chengbin Deng

item.title: Fuji: The Shape, Composition, and Spread of Demand Bursts on Robinhood Chain
item.description: arXiv:2610.35738v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Demand on blockchain-based marketplaces arrives in bursts and at a high rate. On these platforms the data are completely visible, which makes it feasible to compare the bursty demand against the usual load. The congestion manifests as an increased demand for gas, the primary resource a blockchain sells. Existing studies consider how to price the gas. The demand itself, and what it is made of during bursts, has not been measured. We measure it on Robinhood Chain, a layer-2 blockchain that quickly became a venue for trading tokenized equities and memecoins. We collected the data from every block of its first three active months and more than 50 million Uniswap swaps that occurred during bursty periods. We find that a burst trades about as many pools as a quiet period, mostly different ones, and trades them harder, on top of elevated demand that accumulated for hours. With the bursts aligned on their peaks, the median peak is 2.5 times the usual load. Both the rise and the fall of the demand are described by the sum of two exponential functions with different timescales, a slow one of hours and a fast one of minutes. Against a matched quiet period, a burst has 1.05 times the pools, 1.40 times the trades, and 1.21 times the senders. We use two models to explain the arrival of bursts: externally triggered cascades and self-excitation. The former fits the data relatively better. Inside a burst, the entry of each trader into a pool is followed for about 24 seconds by more entries than the existing traders predict. Whether this is because of imitation or because of a shared signal is left open.
item.dc:creator: Pranay Anchuri (Offchain Labs)

item.title: An openly available OpenStreetMap-to-Foursquare category benchmark for points of interest
item.description: arXiv:2511.13369v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The heterogeneity of Point of Interest (POI) taxonomies is a persistent challenge for the integration of urban datasets and the development of location-based services. OpenStreetMap (OSM) adopts a flexible, community-driven tagging system, while Foursquare (FS) relies on a curated hierarchical structure. Here we present an openly available benchmark and mapping framework that aligns OSM tags with the FS taxonomy. This resource integrates the richness of community-driven OSM data with the hierarchical structure of FS, enabling reproducible and interoperable urban analytics. The dataset is complemented by an evaluation of embedding and LLM-based alignment strategies and a pipeline that supports scalable updates as OSM evolves. Together, these elements provide both a robust reference resource and a practical tool for the community. Our approach is structured around three components: the construction of a manually curated benchmark as a gold standard, the evaluation of pretrained text embedding models for semantic alignment between OSM tags and FS categories, and an LLM-based refinement stage that enhances robustness and adaptability. The proposed methodology provides a scalable and reproducible solution for taxonomy unification, with direct applications to urban analytics, mobility studies, and smart city services.
item.dc:creator: Lilou Soulas, Lorenzo Lucchini, Maurizio Napolitano, Sebastiano Bontorin, Simone Centellegher, Bruno Lepri, Riccardo Gallotti, Eleonora Andreotti

item.title: GTIN: A Unified Scalable Framework for Joint Event and Time Prediction in Temporal Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2607.23556v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Temporal graphs are increasingly used to model dynamic systems across diverse domains, including social, financial, and traffic networks. Predicting both what the next event will be and when it will occur in these systems is crucial for understanding and anticipating complex behaviors, but has not been studied much yet, especially in large-scale graphs. To address this gap, we propose a scalable unified mathematical framework that captures varying degrees of complexity across temporal graphs with events occurring on the edges. Our framework is flexible and expressive enough to accommodate a wide range of network structures and temporal dynamics. Building upon this analysis, we introduce our novel scalable approach for jointly predicting the next event and its occurrence time. Empirical evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing techniques, particularly in scenarios involving irregular event patterns and complex temporal dependencies. These findings highlight the potential of our framework as a robust foundation for future research in temporal event prediction.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Ostadmohammadi, Sepehr Kazemi, Hamid R. Rabiee

item.title: Scam Town: Can Scam Education Spread Like a Vaccine?
item.description: arXiv:2610.25040v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Most older adults who hear a warning about scams hear it from someone they know: a relative, a neighbour, or a friend who was targeted. Yet research on scam prevention almost always studies one person at a time. We ask whether scam awareness can spread through a community and protect it the way a vaccine does, since a warning protects whoever hears it and can be passed on. To find out, we built Scam Town, a simulated community in which a large language model plays each resident. Scam centres phone the residents, and after a call a resident can warn the people they know. Word of mouth helped, but it did not take off on its own: each warning led to fewer than one more, so a community cannot count on warnings "going viral". Across 80 simulated towns, everyday talk cut the number of people scammed by roughly a fifth. The largest gains came when an official warning, from a bank, a senior centre, or an agency, reached most of a town and residents then talked about it: in simulation (a combination we did not test live) the two together cut scams by about half. Protection was greatest when warnings reached the people scammers actually call, who here were older residents. Because our residents are language-model stand-ins rather than real people, we treat these findings as predictions to test with people, not as proof. They point to a simple recipe for scam education: give people a clear story they can retell, design campaigns to be passed along, and reach first those most likely to be called.
item.dc:creator: Simiao Ren, Tommy Duong, Xingyu Shen, Jiaqi Gan, Tsang Ng, Ankit Raj, Kidus Zewde, Huaiyu Guo, Siyu Zhang

item.title: Label Ensemble Perspective for Reduced-Complexity Graph Node Classification under Label Noise
item.description: arXiv:2411.11020v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been widely employed for semi-supervised node classification tasks on graphs. However, the performance of GNNs is significantly affected by \emph{label noise}, that is, a small amount of incorrectly labeled nodes can substantially misguide model training. Mainstream solutions define node classification with label noise (NCLN) as a reliable labeling task, often introducing node similarity with quadratic computational complexity to more accurately assess label reliability. To this end, in this paper, we introduce the Label Ensemble Graph Neural Network (LEGNN), a lower complexity method for robust GNNs training against label noise. LEGNN reframes NCLN as a label ensemble task, gathering informative multiple labels instead of constructing a single reliable label, avoiding high-complexity computations for reliability assessment. Specifically, LEGNN conducts a two-step process: bootstrapping neighboring contexts and robust learning with gathered multiple labels. In the former step, we apply random neighbor masks for each node and gather the predicted labels as a high-probability label set. This mitigates the impact of inaccurately labeled neighbors and diversifies the label set. In the latter step, we utilize a partial label learning based strategy to aggregate the high-probability label information for model training. Additionally, we symmetrically gather a low-probability label set to counteract potential noise from the high-probability label set. Extensive experiments on six datasets demonstrate that LEGNN achieves strong classification performance while maintaining computational efficiency. Moreover, it exhibits good scalability on datasets with over one hundred thousand nodes and one million edges.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Rui Zhao, Bin Shi, Zhiming Liang, Jianfei Ruan, Kai Sun, Bo Dong, and Lu Lin. Label ensemble perspective for reduced-complexity graph node classification under label noise. Pattern Recognition, 2026, Article 115169
item.dc:creator: Rui Zhao, Bin Shi, Zhiming Liang, Jianfei Ruan, Kai Sun, Bo Dong, Lu Lin

item.title: Fundamental limits to identifying node and tie memory in temporal networks: marginal artefacts and spreading dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2609.10399v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Temporal-network models place the memory seen in contact data either on nodes, through self-excitation (branching ratio n_node), or on ties, through reinforcement (kappa). The two choices reproduce the same coarse statistics but predict different epidemics. We ask whether contact data can tell them apart and find two limits. The first is attribution. When the initiator of every event is recorded, the likelihood factorises into a timing block containing n_node and a selection block containing kappa, so the two are estimated independently. When it is not, as in proximity data, a missing-information term couples them, with a size set by the entropy of the initiator posterior. The second issue is interpretation. Even where the mechanisms separate, the fitted n_node might not accurately measure memory and it may be set by the distribution of waiting times between events. Shuffling each node's inter-event order, which keeps that distribution, typically changes the estimated n_node by less than 10%; this is a bias that longer records and a flexible scale-free kernel do not remove. Whether node memory is present must therefore be decided by model-free statistics, which find only weak order memory in the proximity records, far less than the fitted n_node around 0.9 would imply. Tie reinforcement remains recoverable, although a latent initiator inflates it by 28%-45%. The two limits lead to two recommendations: record who initiates each contact, and test a fitted node memory against shuffled and model-free benchmarks before interpreting it. On a high-school record, simulating from the fitted node memory under-predicts outbreak sizes by up to a factor of 2, whereas keeping tie reinforcement alone is closer at low transmissibility but overshoots at high.
item.dc:creator: Michele Tizzani

item.title: Projected Effects of Naloxone and Buprenorphine Scale-Up on Opioid Overdose Mortality in Six Pennsylvania Counties
item.description: arXiv:2609.22419v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Opioid overdose deaths remain a severe public health crisis in the US, with heterogeneous burden across counties that differ in epidemic trajectory, baseline resources, and local context. While harm reduction through naloxone distribution and buprenorphine treatment are both evidence-based strategies, limited information on county-level effects hinders the ability of policymakers to prioritize resources across counties. We developed a simulation model of opioid use disorder (OUD), calibrated separately to six Pennsylvania counties spanning large urban (Allegheny, Philadelphia), intermediate-sized (Erie, Dauphin), and rural (Clearfield, Columbia) settings. We projected county-specific overdose mortality trajectories under three levels of increase in buprenorphine dispensing and naloxone distribution (10%, 20%, and 30% above each county's baseline), over a five-year horizon from 2025 to 2029. A 30% increase in naloxone distribution above projected county baseline levels was projected to reduce 2029 overdose deaths by approximately 70% (95% uncertainty interval, UI: 55-81%) in Allegheny County, 11% (95% UI: 4-17%) in Erie County, and 28% (95% UI: 2-64%) in Clearfield County. The relative projected benefits of naloxone and buprenorphine varied by county; buprenorphine produced larger reductions in Erie and Dauphin. The same proportional increase in naloxone distribution produced substantially different projected mortality reductions across the six Pennsylvania counties. County-level context is important for informing harm reduction and treatment prioritization at the county level.
item.dc:creator: Abdulrahman A. Ahmed, M. Amin Rahimian, Qiushi Chen, Praveen Kumar

item.title: A learner-free swarm reaches the explore-exploit equilibrium: A self-organized attractor approximating the reinforcement-learning solution
item.description: arXiv:2610.25113v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The explore-exploit trade-off is the core problem of reinforcement learning (RL). In its multi-agent, resource-sharing form the optimum is not a scalar-return maximum but an equilibrium allocation -- the ideal-free distribution (IFD), the Nash equilibrium of a congestion game. We show that a minimal foraging swarm reaches the shape of this equilibrium as a self-organized attractor -- foragers in proportion to resource richness (matching slope 0.94) -- with no learner, no trained parameters, and no payoff or reward read anywhere in its dynamics. Agents explore by heavy-tailed (Levy) flights, recruit neighbours to a discovery through a threshold cascade on their proximity network, and disperse as a patch crowds; removing the coupling of recruitment to movement collapses the matching (slope 0.08). The reinforcement learning is at the level of the problem and the allocation reached, not the micro-rule. The swarm reaches this equilibrium rather than learning it, attaining its shape but not the exact equilibrium: it stays measurably exploitable (Nash-gap 0.58 versus ~0.01 for a converged learner). Against PPO learners (feedforward, centralized-critic, and graph message-passing) trained in the same sensing-limited environment, the reward-free swarm at zero training matches the IFD gradient more faithfully than any learner (slope ~1 vs 0.69-0.91) and ties the best learner's harvest where clustered (both plateau at ~0.80 of an oracle ceiling), while the learner collects more where resource is scarce (0.33 vs 0.22) and holds tighter per-capita intake. Learning thus buys precision and transfer, not a better allocation; neither message passing nor a centralized critic exceeds it at this budget. We read this not as beating RL, but as evidence that a minimal swarm's physics reaches the equilibrium RL seeks without a learner, a reward, or a trained parameter. A companion paper develops the mechanism.
item.dc:creator: Galen J. Wilkerson
